hints: Look closely at the two sugars in the diagram. Notice one is upside-down compared to the other, and they are joined by an O bridge in the middle.
Remember which polysaccharide also has its glucose monomers flipped alternately to make long, straight, strong chains for support, and which ones use the same-way-up alpha glucose for storage.
walkthrough:
**Observe the chitin diagram**

Look at the two ring sugars. The left one has CH2OH on top, the right one has CH2OH on the bottom.

That tells you every second monomer is rotated 180 degrees. They are linked by a glycosidic bond through an oxygen atom.

**Recall what makes cellulose special**

Cellulose is made of beta-glucose joined by 1,4 glycosidic bonds.

Because it is beta-glucose, each monomer must flip over to bond. This gives long, straight, unbranched chains that pack together with hydrogen bonds for great strength.

**Compare structural versus storage roles**

Chitin is described as structural, for hard outer shells. That is a support job, just like cellulose in plant cell walls.

Amylopectin, amylose and glycogen are all storage molecules made of alpha-glucose. They form helical or branched shapes for easy hydrolysis, not straight structural fibres. So cellulose is most like chitin.

options.A: Amylopectin is a storage polysaccharide of alpha-glucose with 1,4 and 1,6 branches for plants. It is coiled and branched, not a straight structural chain like chitin.
options.B: Amylose is a storage polysaccharide of alpha-glucose with 1,4 links that forms a helix. It is for energy storage, not for strength, so it does not match the flipped, straight pattern.
options.C: Cellulose is correct because it also has unbranched chains with alternate monomers flipped 180 degrees joined by 1,4 glycosidic bonds, forming strong straight fibres for structural support.
options.D: Glycogen is a highly branched storage polysaccharide of alpha-glucose in animals. Its many branches suit rapid mobilisation, not the straight structural role of chitin.
